q: How many flavours of quark are there in the standard model?
x: There are six quark flavours: up, down, strange, charm, bottom and top. Counting only the three quarks inside a proton or neutron gives the tempting 3.

q: A baryon is made of two up quarks and one strange quark. What is its charge? (e = charge of a proton)
x: Charges: u = +⅔e, s = −⅓e, so ⅔ + ⅔ − ⅓ = +1, charge +e. Taking the strange quark as +⅓e gives +(5/3)e.

q: A meson consists of an up quark and an anti-down quark. What is its charge?
x: u has +⅔e; the anti-down quark has the opposite of d's −⅓e, i.e. +⅓e. Total = ⅔ + ⅓ = +e (this is the π⁺). Forgetting that the antiquark's charge is reversed gives ⅔ − ⅓ = +⅓e.
Mesons are quark–antiquark pairs; baryons are three quarks, and antibaryons are three antiquarks. Three quarks is the baryon description and the usual mix-up.

q: Which of these particles is a lepton?
x: Leptons (electron, muon, tau and their neutrinos) are fundamental and contain no quarks. Proton and neutron are baryons and the pion is a meson, all made of quarks.

q: A hadron has zero charge and zero baryon number. Which quark content is possible for it?
x: Zero baryon number needs a quark–antiquark pair (a meson); u ū has charge ⅔ − ⅔ = 0. u d d has charge 0 but baryon number 1 (the neutron); u d̄ has charge +e and ū d has −e.

q: Which particle carries the electromagnetic force?
x: The photon is the exchange particle of the electromagnetic force. Gluons carry the strong force and W and Z bosons the weak force.

q: The strong force that holds quarks together inside a proton is carried by:
x: Gluons are the exchange particles of the strong force between quarks. Photons carry the electromagnetic force, which is the common wrong choice.

q: Which statement about the carriers of the weak force is correct?
o: They are the W⁺, W⁻ and Z⁰ bosons, which are massive, so the weak force has a very short range
They are massless W and Z bosons, so the weak force has an infinite range
They are photons, so the weak force acts only on charged particles
They are gluons, so the weak force acts only between quarks
x: The weak force is carried by W⁺, W⁻ and Z⁰ bosons; they are very massive, which makes the range of the weak force extremely short. Massless carriers (photon) give long range, as for electromagnetism.

q: Which list puts the four fundamental forces in order of DECREASING strength?
x: The strong force is strongest, then electromagnetic (about 1/100 of strong), then weak, and gravity is by far the weakest. Putting weak above electromagnetic is the usual slip.

q: What is the role of the Higgs boson in the standard model?
o: It carries the strong force between quarks
It is linked to the field that gives elementary particles such as W and Z bosons their mass
It binds electrons to the nucleus
x: The Higgs boson is the particle of the Higgs field, through which elementary particles (including W and Z bosons, quarks and leptons) acquire mass. It is not a carrier of the strong force (gluons) or electromagnetism (photons).

q: In β⁻ decay, what happens at the quark level inside the nucleus?
o: An up quark changes into a down quark
A down quark changes into an up quark
A down quark changes into a strange quark
A gluon changes into an electron
x: In β⁻ decay a neutron (udd) becomes a proton (uud): one d quark changes into a u quark, emitting a W⁻ that gives an electron and an antineutrino. u → d is β⁺ decay.

q: In β⁺ decay, besides the daughter nucleus, the particles emitted are:
o: an electron and an electron antineutrino
a positron and an electron antineutrino
a positron and an electron neutrino
an electron and an electron neutrino
x: In β⁺ decay a proton becomes a neutron (u → d), giving a positron and an electron neutrino; lepton number is conserved (−1 + 1 = 0). The antineutrino goes with the electron in β⁻ decay.

q: A carbon-14 nucleus (6 protons, 8 neutrons) undergoes β⁻ decay. How do the total numbers of up and down quarks in the nucleus change?
o: Up quarks decrease by 1, down quarks increase by 1
Up quarks increase by 1, down quarks stay the same
Up quarks increase by 1, down quarks decrease by 1
x: Before: u = 6×2 + 8×1 = 20, d = 6×1 + 8×2 = 22. After (7 protons, 7 neutrons): u = 14 + 7 = 21, d = 7 + 14 = 21. So one d became one u; reversing it is the β⁺ case.

q: Which observation in β⁻ decay led to the proposal of the neutrino?
o: All the emitted electrons have exactly the same energy
The emitted electrons have a continuous range of kinetic energies
The daughter nucleus has the same atomic number as the parent
An alpha particle is always emitted with the electron
x: If only the electron and the nucleus shared the energy, every electron would have the same energy; the observed continuous spectrum meant a third, neutral particle (the neutrino) carries away part of the energy and momentum.
